scope.start: 18a: what the Rabbis of Rav Amram's baraita hold about the heifer brought by two equidistant towns (the page opens mid-exchange)
scope.end: 19a: the conclusion that each of the three cases of R. Akiva's ruling had to be taught

sections.title: One Heifer on Condition: The Rabbis Hold *I Efshar Le'tzamtzem* Even in Human Hands
sections.gist: Continuing the question of what the Rabbis hold about matters in human hands: their ruling of one jointly brought heifer shows that even measured distances can't be taken as exactly equal.

bullets.text: In Rav Amram's baraita, R. Eliezer has the two towns bring two heifers. The Rabbis have them bring one heifer in partnership, stipulating that it is for whichever town is really nearer.

The Gemara reasons from the Rabbis' ruling. If they held that precision is possible and that *kerovah* includes *kerovot*, they would require two heifers. If they read *kerovah* as excluding *kerovot*, they would require none.
One heifer brought on condition only makes sense if one town must really be nearer. So the Rabbis hold *i efshar le'tzamtzem*, even for matters in human hands, and the Gemara accepts this conclusion.
On the physical level there is never true simultaneity: a finer instrument will always reveal some difference.

The legal question is whether a measurement can be trusted. Halakha normally relies on a careful measurement, such as a *kezayit* or a *tefach*. A claim of perfectly equal distances or perfect simultaneity is so extraordinary that the Rabbis assume an error was made. This is a carve-out for one kind of claim, not general doubt about measuring.

Tosafot (17b) surveys the sugyot across Shas for the ruling. One possibility is to follow the Rabbis for matters in Heaven's hands and R. Yosei HaGelili for matters in human hands. The other is to follow the Rabbis in both.

sections.title: Two Males from One Ewe: Better or Leaner, *matanot kehunah*, One Lamb Dies
sections.gist: The Gemara works through the earlier Mishnah clause by clause: which lamb the priest takes, whether the owner owes *matanot kehunah* (priestly gifts) from the lamb he keeps, and what happens when one lamb dies.

chart.caption: Two possibly-firstborn lambs: what each view gives the priest
rows: The healthier one presumably emerged first
The survivor stays with the owner
*Ha'motzi me'chavero alav ha'ra'ayah*: the burden of proof is on the claimant

children.title: Better or Leaner Lamb: R. Tarfon's Presumption vs. R. Akiva's *Meshamenin*
children.gist: R. Tarfon gives the priest the better lamb because the healthier one came out first. R. Yochanan reads R. Akiva's *meshamenin* as giving the priest the leaner one, and proves it from the Mishnah's latter clause.

bullets.text: Mishnah (17a–b): a ewe bearing for the first time gives birth to two males whose heads emerged as one. R. Tarfon: the priest chooses the better one. His reasoning: the healthier and better lamb is presumed to have emerged first.
The Gemara doesn't say whether this presumption makes the lamb a certain *bekhor* or only gives the priest a monetary claim. Perhaps it is left open because R. Tarfon later retracts.
R. Akiva: "they assess (*meshamenin*) between them." R. Chiyya bar Abba in the name of R. Yochanan: according to R. Akiva, the priest takes the leaner lamb.
R. Chiyya bar Abba objects: *meshamenin* sounds like dividing the value. R. Yochanan replies: "While you were eating dates in Babylonia, we in Eretz Yisrael explained it from the latter clause."

The latter clause: if one lamb died, R. Akiva leaves the survivor with the owner, by *ha'motzi me'chavero alav ha'ra'ayah*. If R. Akiva meant dividing the value, he would divide the survivor there too.
So *meshamenin* means that the extra fat (*shuman*) of the better lamb is what is in dispute. The owner tells the priest: "Bring proof that the better one is the firstborn, and take it."

The reading is admittedly forced, and only the latter clause compels it. R. Tarfon's two clauses clash in the same way, and one might try to read the Mishnah on its own terms, as the Vilna Gaon sometimes does.
Neither lamb is certainly the *bekhor*, so the priest's lamb, like the owner's, must develop a blemish before it is eaten (Rashi).

illustration.caption: The Mishnah's two lambs from one ewe (18a). R. Tarfon gives the better lamb to the priest; R. Akiva, as R. Yochanan reads him, gives the priest the leaner one and leaves the extra fat in dispute.

children.title: *Matanot kehunah* from the Kept Lamb: R. Meir vs. R. Yosei
children.gist: Three steps: R. Meir's two-sided claim against R. Yosei's fictive exchange, R. Elazar on a case with no replacement, and Rav Pappa on an animal of uncertain tithe status.

chart.caption: When must the owner give *matanot kehunah* from a doubtful animal?
columns: Uncertain *bekhor*, priest got nothing (male and female)
rows: The priest comes from two sides
As if the priest acquired the lamb and sold it back

children.title: Two-Sided Claim or *Asu She'eino Zokheh Ke'zokheh*?
children.gist: R. Meir obligates because the priest wins either way. R. Yosei exempts because the kept lamb is treated as if the priest had acquired it and sold it back.

bullets.text: Mishnah: the second lamb grazes until it becomes blemished. When the owner slaughters it he must give the *matanot kehunah* (foreleg, jaw and maw). R. Yosei exempts him.
The first opinion is identified as R. Meir's because the later Mishnah (18b) names him.
R. Yochanan explains R. Meir: the priest comes at the owner from two sides. "If it is the firstborn, it is all mine. If not, at least give me the priestly gifts."

Rava explains R. Yosei: *asu she'eino zokheh ke'zokheh*. The kept lamb is treated as though it entered the priest's possession and he sold it to the owner, blemished, in exchange for the lamb he received.
So the owner can say: "Perhaps this is the firstborn, and I have already given it to the priest." A firstborn bought from a priest owes no gifts.

The fiction is needed because the claim concerns a specific animal, not only its value. The kept lamb itself may be the priest's, so handing over the leaner lamb as payment wouldn't settle that on its own.

illustration.caption: Rava's explanation of R. Yosei (18a): the leaner lamb goes to the priest in fact, while the better lamb is treated as if it passed to him and was sold back to the owner blemished. Below, the two sides of the dispute.

children.title: R. Elazar: No Replacement with the Priest, Gifts Owed; Exchange, Not a Decree
children.gist: All agree that the gifts are owed when the priest received nothing. The Gemara defends the need for this statement twice, establishing that the exchange is R. Yosei's own reason and not a decree against shearing and labor.

bullets.text: R. Elazar: all agree that an uncertain *bekhor* whose replacement is not in the priest's possession owes the *matanot kehunah*. An example is a male and a female born together, where the priest receives nothing.

Challenge: if "all" includes R. Yosei, this is obvious. He exempts only where the replacement is with the priest, as *asu she'eino zokheh ke'zokheh*, and without a replacement that reasoning doesn't apply.

Answer: it is needed lest you say that R. Yosei exempts from a different concern. Obligating the gifts might lead the owner to treat the animal as fully non-sacred and shear it or work it, and that concern would apply even with no replacement.
Objection: the later Mishnah has R. Yosei say that any animal whose replacements (*chalifin be'yad kohen*) are in the priest's possession is exempt. So without a replacement he obligates.

Answer: the statement is still needed, lest you say R. Yosei was arguing on R. Meir's terms. "I exempt even without a replacement, for fear of shearing and labor; but at least concede where the replacement is with the priest." R. Meir refused even that.
R. Elazar teaches that the *chalifin be'yad kohen* (replacement in the priest's possession) really is R. Yosei's own reason.

children.title: Rav Pappa: Uncertain Tithe Is Exempt; Principle, Not 'Lest the Gifts Be Forgotten'
children.gist: All agree that an animal of uncertain tithe status owes no gifts. This shows that R. Meir obligates only because of the two-sided claim, not to keep the gifts from being forgotten.

bullets.text: Rav Pappa: all agree that an animal of uncertain *ma'aser behemah* status is exempt from the *matanot kehunah*.

The case: the tenth animal becomes mixed with another. Both wait for a blemish and the owner eats them. The priest has no two-sided claim, since if this one is the tithe it was never his, and the owner can simply say "perhaps this is the tithe."
Challenge: if "all" includes R. Meir, this is obvious. His reason is the priest's two-sided claim, which is absent here.
Answer: it is needed lest you say that R. Meir obligates so that the category of *matanot kehunah* won't be forgotten. That concern would apply to uncertain tithe as well.

Objection: the later Mishnah frames their dispute around a *chalifin be'yad kohen*, that is, whether one who didn't acquire is treated as having acquired. It says nothing about keeping the gifts from being forgotten.

Answer: one could say the Mishnah chose the replacement case only to show how far R. Yosei goes, exempting even where the priest comes from two sides, while R. Meir obligates even an uncertain tithe. Rav Pappa teaches that R. Meir in fact exempts the uncertain tithe.
The upshot: the dispute is argued on the merits of the law (*al pi din*) on both sides, not as a protective measure.

children.title: One Lamb Died: *Yachloku* or *Ha'motzi Me'chavero*?
children.gist: Three steps: R. Tarfon's retraction, R. Chiyya's two parables, and Rava's (or Rav Pappa's) placing of the dispute in a priest who shepherds in the owner's courtyard.

chart.caption: Who holds the surviving animal, and who must prove?
columns: Deposit with a homeowner who has his own sheep
Priest as shepherd in the owner's courtyard
rows: The owner transfers part of his courtyard to the priest
The owner, who stands to lose, transfers nothing

children.title: R. Tarfon Retracted: Divide in Every Case
children.gist: R. Tarfon's *yachloku* contradicts his presumption that the better lamb is the firstborn, so R. Ami says he retracted it.

bullets.text: Mishnah: if one lamb died, R. Tarfon rules *yachloku*: they divide the survivor.
The Gemara asks why. By his presumption, if the better lamb died it was the priest's and the survivor is the owner's. If the leaner one died, the survivor is the priest's.
R. Ami: R. Tarfon retracted (*chazar bo*) and ruled that they divide in all cases. The Mishnah was not revised to reflect the change.

returns_to.note: Revisits R. Tarfon's first ruling, that the priest takes the better lamb

children.title: R. Chiyya's Parables: Shepherd Between Two Owners vs. Homeowner's Flock
children.gist: R. Akiva leaves the survivor with the owner. R. Chiyya compares R. Tarfon's view to a shepherd holding two depositors' sheep, and R. Akiva's to a homeowner holding a deposit among his own sheep.

bullets.text: R. Akiva: the survivor stays with the owner, since *ha'motzi me'chavero alav ha'ra'ayah*.

R. Chiyya's parable for R. Tarfon: two people each deposit a sheep with a shepherd, and one sheep dies with its owner unknown. The shepherd places the survivor between them and withdraws, and they divide it. Here too the live lamb is in the possession of neither side.

His parable for R. Akiva: someone deposits a sheep with a homeowner who has sheep of his own, and it is unknown whose sheep died. The claimant must prove his claim. Here too the live lamb is in the owner's possession.

children.title: The Real Dispute: A Priest Shepherding in the Owner's Courtyard
children.gist: Both parables are agreed. R. Tarfon and R. Akiva argue only over whether an owner implicitly transfers part of his courtyard to a priest who serves as his shepherd.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks: if they speak of different circumstances, what do they disagree about? Surely neither rejects the other's parable.
Rava (some say Rav Pappa): all agree to both parables. They disagree where the lambs were born in the owner's courtyard and the shepherd is a priest to whom the owner usually gives his firstborns.

R. Tarfon: the owner transfers part of his courtyard to the priest so that he acquires the firstborn there (*kinyan chatzer*), since the owner wants the mitzvah done. The priest has partial jurisdiction, as in the shepherd case, so they divide.
R. Akiva: since the owner stands to lose in a case of doubt, he transfers nothing. The courtyard is his alone, as in the homeowner case, so the claimant must prove.
So the Mishnah is not an ordinary birth in the owner's hands, where all would put the burden of proof on the priest. It is specifically a priest-shepherd arrangement.

sections.title: Mishnah: Two Ewes—Males, Females, and a Ewe That Bore Before
sections.gist: The same rulings applied to two ewes: when both are bearing for the first time, and when one of them has borne before. In some cases the priest gets nothing.

children.title: Two First-Time Ewes: Both Males, One Male, or Nothing
children.gist: Each firstborn male goes to the priest. Where it is unclear which male is the firstborn, the rulings of the one-ewe case repeat. Where a female may have come first from each ewe, the priest gets nothing.

bullets.text: Two ewes bearing for the first time bear two males: both go to the priest. A male and a female: the male goes to the priest. Each is its mother's firstborn.

Two males and a female: one male is the owner's and one the priest's. R. Tarfon: the priest chooses the better. R. Akiva: they assess, and the priest takes the leaner. The second lamb grazes until it becomes blemished.
The owner owes the *matanot kehunah* from it, and R. Yosei exempts him. If one lamb died, R. Tarfon: they divide. R. Akiva: *ha'motzi me'chavero alav ha'ra'ayah*.
Two females and a male, or two males and two females: the priest gets nothing, since perhaps both ewes bore females first.

children.title: One Ewe Bore Before: Disputed Male, or Nothing for the Priest
children.gist: Only the first-time ewe can bear a firstborn now. Two males repeat the dispute, and here R. Yosei states his principle of the *chalifin be'yad kohen*; a male and a female give the priest nothing.

bullets.text: One ewe has borne before and one has not, and they bear two males. One male is the owner's and one the priest's. R. Tarfon: the priest chooses the better. R. Akiva: the priest takes the leaner. The second lamb grazes until it becomes blemished.

The owner owes the *matanot kehunah*. R. Yosei exempts him: "any animal whose replacements are in the priest's possession (*kol she'chalifin be'yad kohen*) is exempt from the priestly gifts." R. Meir obligates.
If one lamb died, R. Tarfon: they divide. R. Akiva: the claimant must prove.
A male and a female: all agree the priest gets nothing, since perhaps the ewe that bore before bore the male and the first-time ewe bore the female.
This is the clause the Gemara cited earlier: here the Mishnah states R. Yosei's reason and names R. Meir explicitly.

sections.title: Why Three Cases? *Tzerikha*: Strength Never Proves Birth Order
sections.gist: All three cases in which R. Akiva gives the priest the leaner lamb are needed. In each, the better lamb's origin might have seemed provable from its strength, and R. Akiva still doesn't concede.

bullets.text: This Mishnah and the previous one give three cases in which R. Akiva gives the priest the leaner lamb and R. Tarfon the better one. The Gemara says each was necessary.
From the first case alone (one ewe, two males), one might limit R. Akiva to it. Both came from one womb, so there is no reason to think the better one came first.
The second case (two first-time ewes, two males and a female): one might think R. Akiva concedes that the better male is the one from the ewe that bore a single lamb.

From the second case alone, one might limit him to two first-time ewes. Where one ewe had borne before, one might think he concedes that the first-time ewe's offspring is the superior one. So each case is needed.
Taken together, the cases teach that for R. Akiva, size or health never counts as proof of which lamb is the firstborn, however suggestive it seems.
Rashi: the R. Tarfon meant here is the R. Tarfon of the Mishnah's opening clause (the priest chooses the better), not the R. Tarfon who retracted and divides.

returns_to.note: Returns to R. Akiva's ruling that the priest takes the leaner lamb

key_terms.sense: whether two things can coincide exactly
key_terms.definition: The question of whether two events or measurements can be exactly equal, such as a simultaneous birth or two identical distances. One who holds "i efshar le'tzamtzem" treats such exact equality as impossible, so one of the two must really have come first or be nearer.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Rabbis' ruling of one heifer brought on condition shows they hold i efshar le'tzamtzem even for matters in human hands.

key_terms.sense: burden of proof on the claimant
key_terms.definition: The principle that one who seeks to take property from another's possession must prove his claim; without proof, the property stays with its holder.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Akiva's basis for giving the priest the leaner lamb and leaving the survivor with the owner; its application depends on whether the priest-shepherd holds part of the courtyard.

key_terms.sense: the priestly gifts from a slaughtered animal
key_terms.definition: The foreleg, jaw and maw of a non-sacred animal, which must be given to a priest when it is slaughtered.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Meir and R. Yosei dispute whether the owner must give them from the possibly-firstborn lamb he keeps.

key_terms.sense: treating one who didn't acquire as if he did
key_terms.definition: A rabbinic legal construction by which a party who never formally took possession is treated as though he had acquired an item.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava's explanation of R. Yosei: the kept lamb is treated as if it entered the priest's possession and was sold back to the owner, so no gifts are owed.

key_terms.sense: a replacement held by the priest
key_terms.definition: A case where the priest has received one animal in place of a doubtful one, so that the animal kept by the owner may be regarded as having been exchanged with the priest.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yosei exempts from the priestly gifts only where such a replacement is in the priest's possession; R. Elazar says that without one, even he obligates.

key_terms.sense: an animal of uncertain firstborn status
key_terms.definition: An animal that may or may not be a firstborn. It may not be used or eaten until it becomes blemished, and questions arise over what the priest may claim from it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The lamb the owner keeps is an uncertain firstborn, which gives the priest his two-sided claim to the gifts.

key_terms.definition: Every tenth animal born in a herd or flock, which is consecrated. It belongs to its owner, and once it becomes blemished the owner may eat it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Pappa: all agree that an animal of uncertain tithe status owes no priestly gifts, showing that R. Meir's obligation rests on the two-sided claim.

key_terms.definition: A person's courtyard or property acquires on his behalf items that come into it, even without his physical taking.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Tarfon holds that the owner transfers part of his courtyard to the priest-shepherd so that the priest can acquire a firstborn born there.

judgment_calls: The page opens mid-way through the heifer discussion. The Rabbis' conclusion (18a.6) could be a child of the previous daf's section on the heifer; it is a top-level section here because it is the scope's first line and closes the whole precision question.

18a.7–18b.12 are grouped under one parent because the Gemara goes clause by clause through the same Mishnah and its latter clause drives the reading of the first. Three top-level sections (lambs, gifts, death) would also work.
R. Elazar's objection from the later Mishnah and its answer, that R. Yosei was arguing on R. Meir's terms (18a.15–18b.2), are kept under R. Elazar, where they fall in the text, not under Rav Pappa.
The *tzerikha* passage (18b.17–19a.1) is a separate top-level section and not a child of the new Mishnah, since it concerns both Mishnayot.
The new Mishnah is split into two children by ewe configuration (both first-time vs. one bore before). It could have been one section with bullets.
coverage_notes: The shiur's material on 18a.1–18a.5 (R. Eliezer holding like R. Yosei HaGelili, the first baraita's first tanna and the *kerovah/kerovot* dispute) falls before this outline's scope and is left out, except as background in the s1 chart. The previous daf's essay tail covers 17b.
The essay says the Gemara concludes the matter is a dispute among *tanna'im*. The text (18a.6) concludes that the Rabbis hold *i efshar le'tzamtzem* even in human hands. Followed the text.
The essay places the 'Rabbi Yosei spoke on Rabbi Meir's terms' answer in the Rav Pappa section. The text gives it at 18b.2, as the defense of R. Elazar's statement. Followed the text's order.

The essay says the Gemara rejects the 'lest the gifts be forgotten' reading of R. Meir from the latter clause. The text raises that objection and answers it: the Mishnah may have used the replacement case only to show how far R. Yosei goes, and Rav Pappa teaches that R. Meir exempts uncertain tithe. Followed the text.
The essay says the priest who can't prove his claim 'receives the dead one' under R. Akiva. The text says only that the survivor stays with the owner. Followed the text.
The essay attributes the two parables to 'the Gemara'. The text gives them in the name of R. Chiyya. Followed the text.
The essay spells R. Yosei HaGelili as 'Yose'. Used the text's spelling.
